analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2003 cuts to dividend and capital gains tax rates permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the 2003 dividend and capital gains tax cuts permanent never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Paul Ryan introduced a one-page bill repealing the expiration date on the 2003 law that cut the tax rates on dividends and capital gains. Without it, those lower rates were scheduled to end after 2008 and revert to ordinary income tax rates. The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, investors who realize capital gains and receive taxable dividends would keep the reduced rates (15% for most, 5% for lower incomes) permanently rather than seeing them expire. Because capital gains and dividend income is concentrated among high-income households, the bulk of the benefit in dollar terms would go to households at the top of the income distribution, and asset holders would face less tax-driven pressure to sell holdings. The cost would fall on the federal Treasury, meaning either higher taxes elsewhere, more borrowing, or less spending capacity over time.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sunset provision in the 2003 Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act, making the reduced dividend and capital gains rates permanent instead of expiring after 2008.
Permanently locks in a maximum 15% rate on most long-term capital gains and qualified dividends, shielding investors from the scheduled reversion to ordinary income tax rates.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost: making the rates permanent forecloses the scheduled post-2008 return of higher rates, permanently reducing federal revenue from investment income. That revenue loss would have to be made up through other taxes, more federal borrowing, or lower spending. Within the taxpaying public, wage earners who get little of their income from capital gains or dividends receive essentially nothing from the bill while sharing the fiscal consequences.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and wage taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Capital gains and dividend income flows disproportionately to the wealthiest households, so making the reduced rates permanent is a large, permanent tax benefit concentrated at the top of the income distribution rather than a broad tax cut.
Eliminating the expiration date removes a major source of scheduled federal revenue, increasing deficits or pressuring future Congresses to raise other taxes or cut spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered one narrow thing: permanence for the 2003 investment tax rates. Its benefits were real but heavily concentrated among households with significant investment income, while its cost — the permanent loss of scheduled revenue from those rates — was spread across everyone who depends on or pays into the federal budget. As a transfer of long-term tax value toward wealth holders, the drawbacks outweighed any broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it quietly expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Paul Ryan introduced the bill on July 9, 2004, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Five House Republicans signed on as cosponsors.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded before the end of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the scheduled expiration of the reduced dividend and capital gains rates stayed on the books, preserving that future federal revenue. Investors with large capital gains and dividends did not get the permanence they sought, and no one else gained or lost materially.

for.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2003 dividend and capital gains tax cuts permanent.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican (one sponsor and five Republican cosponsors), but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan division was ever tested on the record.

industries.industry: High-income households and investors in stocks and other appreciated assets
industries.note: The bill would have made the reduced capital gains and dividend rates permanent, a benefit concentrated among top-income households, financed by permanently forgoing federal revenue from investment income. Its death left the scheduled post-2008 rate reversion in place.

Permanently lower taxes on capital gains and dividends would have encouraged trading and made investment products more tax-advantaged, supporting demand for brokerage and fund services, at the cost of Treasury revenue. Because the bill never advanced, these effects never materialized.
